questions.title: Memory Ownership practice 1
questions.prompt: What does `std::move` do to a unique_ptr?
choices: Transfers its ownership to the destination
Copies the owned object automatically
Deletes both pointers
Makes the object global
questions.explanation: Move transfers the unique ownership; the destination owns the object and the source becomes empty.

questions.title: Memory Ownership practice 2
choices: When several parts truly share ownership
For every local integer
Whenever a raw reference is enough
To avoid including memory
questions.explanation: A shared pointer models multiple owners whose lifetimes overlap, not ordinary temporary access to an object.

questions.title: Trace Memory Ownership
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: The unique pointer owns the Student, move transfers that ownership into active, and cleanup happens automatically when active leaves scope. The resulting output is 'Ada'.

questions.title: Memory Ownership practice 5
questions.prompt: What happens to the Student when `student` (a unique_ptr) goes out of scope?
choices: It is destroyed automatically, with no manual delete needed
It leaks unless you call delete student
It is copied, so two Students now exist
It stays alive until the program ends
questions.explanation: A `unique_ptr` owns its object and deletes it when the pointer leaves scope. That is the reason to prefer it over raw `new`: the cleanup is tied to the object's lifetime, so there is no `delete` to forget. A unique_ptr cannot be copied, and the object does not outlive its owner.

questions.title: Shared ownership
questions.prompt: When is `std::shared_ptr` actually a good fit?
choices: When multiple owners genuinely share responsibility for the same object.
Use shared ownership when one clear owner exists.
Call `delete` manually for memory owned by a smart pointer.
Copy a unique owner as if two owners are allowed.
questions.explanation: `shared_ptr` uses reference counting, so it is useful when the ownership model truly has more than one owner. Using it everywhere can hide lifetime design problems and can create cycles that never release.

questions.title: Start with values
questions.prompt: What should C++ code prefer before reaching for manual dynamic allocation?
choices: Use raw `new` and `delete` for ordinary container data.
Prefer values and standard containers first.
Use `shared_ptr` for every local value even when there is one owner.
Allocate every object on the heap before considering a stack value.
questions.explanation: Values and standard containers handle most beginner data without explicit ownership decisions. They clean themselves up, compose well, and avoid many pointer lifetime bugs.

questions.title: Unique ownership
questions.prompt: What helper expresses one dynamic owner clearly?
choices: Create a reference cycle with shared ownership.
Use a dangling pointer after the owner is gone.
Use make_unique for one dynamic owner.
Return a reference to a local object.
questions.explanation: `make_unique` creates an object owned by one `unique_ptr`. That makes ownership transfer explicit and avoids pairing a raw `new` with a later manual `delete`.

questions.title: Moving ownership
questions.prompt: How should code transfer a `unique_ptr` to another owner?
choices: Move unique ownership deliberately.
Copy the `unique_ptr` so both variables own the same object.
Pass the raw pointer and manually delete it in both places.
Keep using the old owner as if nothing changed.
questions.explanation: Move unique ownership deliberately so readers can see that the original owner gives up responsibility. After the move, code should not behave as if the old owner still controls the object.

questions.title: Shared pointer restraint
questions.prompt: Why not use `shared_ptr` for every object?
choices: Use shared ownership only when the model requires it.
Use `shared_ptr` to avoid designing lifetime.
Reset a smart pointer while other code still expects the object.
Mix raw and smart ownership for the same object.
questions.explanation: Shared ownership is a design statement, not a default memory shortcut. If there is one clear owner, values, containers, or `unique_ptr` usually express the lifetime more honestly.

questions.title: Clear responsibility
questions.prompt: What should ownership tools make clear?
choices: Hide who is responsible for deleting the object.
Use automatic lifetime and smart pointers to make resource responsibility clear.
Use manual cleanup when RAII would handle it.
Pass ownership when the function only needs to read.
questions.explanation: Ownership tools should show which object is responsible for lifetime and when cleanup happens. Automatic lifetime, containers, and smart pointers make that responsibility visible without scattered manual `delete` calls.
